title: Simple Random Sampling With and Without Replacement
breadcrumb: Sampling theory → Equal-probability designs → SRSWR and SRSWOR
engineName: Both designs give an unbiased sample mean; without replacement reduces variance through the finite-population correction.
objectives: Distinguish simple random sampling with replacement (SRSWR) from without replacement (SRSWOR).
Calculate the probability of a sample or ordered sequence under each design.
Show that the sample mean and sample proportion are unbiased under both designs.
Derive the variance of the sample mean under SRSWR and SRSWOR.
Apply and interpret the finite-population correction.
Compare the two designs in a small numerical example.

prereq.name: Population and sample mean
prereq.why: The estimator is the arithmetic mean of the selected observations.

prereq.name: Expectation and variance
prereq.why: Unbiasedness and precision are assessed using expectation and variance.

prereq.name: Indicator variables and proportions
prereq.why: A sample proportion is the average of zero-one indicators.

traps: With replacement, the same unit can be selected more than once; the sample is a sequence of draws and repeats count.
Without replacement, every selected unit is distinct.
Both sample means are unbiased for the finite-population mean.
SRSWR draws are independent; SRSWOR draws are dependent.
For SRSWOR, use the finite-population correction (N−n)/(N−1) with the finite-population variance defined using denominator N−1.
Do not say the variance reduction makes the SRSWOR estimator biased; expectation and variance are separate properties.
When n=1, the two variance expressions agree; when n=N, SRSWOR is a census and its variance is zero.
howto: First identify whether a selected unit can appear again. Write the population values and the sampling design. For unbiasedness, use symmetry: every draw or sampled unit has the population mean as its expectation. For variance, use σ²_pop=N⁻¹Σ(y_i−Ȳ)² for SRSWR, or S²=(N−1)⁻¹Σ(y_i−Ȳ)² for SRSWOR. Then V(ȳ_WR)=σ²_pop/n and V(ȳ_WOR)=(1−n/N)S²/n. Equivalently, V(ȳ_WOR)=((N−n)/(N−1))σ²_pop/n. State the variance convention before substituting.

scenes.title: A finite population and a sample
scenes.objective: Set up the quantities used in both designs.
body: Suppose a finite population contains N fixed values y₁,…,y_N. Its population mean is Ȳ=(1/N)Σy_i. We want to estimate this mean by selecting n observations.
A sample mean is ȳ=(1/n)Σ of the n observed values. The sampling design determines which samples can occur and how likely they are.
The population values are fixed. The estimator is random because a different sample can be selected on another repetition of the design.

items.recall: The number of units in the population.
refresh: A finite population contains N distinct units, each with a fixed value y_i for the variable being studied.
The population total is the sum of all these fixed values, and the population mean is that total divided by N.
For example, if the five household values are 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6, the population mean is 4; this target does not change when a sample is drawn.

items.recall: The number of draws or observations in the sample.
refresh: The sample size n tells us how many observations are collected in one repetition of the sampling procedure.
Under sampling with replacement, n counts draws even if the same unit is selected more than once.
Under sampling without replacement, all n observations are distinct population units, so n cannot exceed N.
To calculate the population mean, add the values of every unit in the finite population.
Divide this population total by N, the number of units; do not divide by the sample size.
The sample mean uses only the selected observations and varies from one possible sample to another, while the population mean remains fixed.

ask.q: Why is the sample mean random if the population is fixed?
ask.nudge: Different samples can produce different observed averages.

scenes.title: Two ways to draw the sample
scenes.objective: Explain replacement using a simple analogy.
body: Imagine drawing numbered household cards from a box. With replacement, return each card before the next draw. A household can therefore appear more than once.
Without replacement, keep each drawn card outside the box. No household can appear twice in the sample.
Both are probability sampling designs. The difference changes the dependence between draws and the variance, not the target population mean.

scenario.title: What happens after the first draw?
body: There are five cards labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5, one for each household. We draw two cards to represent a sample of size two.
If card 2 is drawn first and returned to the box, the second draw can again be card 2. The ordered sequence (2,2) is possible under sampling with replacement.
If card 2 is kept out after the first draw, the second draw must be one of the other four cards. The sequence (2,2) is impossible under sampling without replacement.
scenario.q: Which design permits the same household to be selected twice?
scenario.answer: SRSWR, because the selected unit is returned before the next draw.

ask.q: What is the key operational difference?
ask.nudge: Return the selected unit or keep it out.

scenes.title: Probability of selection
scenes.objective: Compare probabilities under the two designs.

blocks.body: Each draw independently selects one of N units with probability 1/N. An ordered sequence of n draws has probability (1/N)^n. Repeated units are allowed.
The first draw has N possible units, the second has N−1, and so on. Each ordered sequence of n distinct units has probability 1/[N(N−1)…(N−n+1)].
For SRSWR there are N^n ordered draw sequences. For SRSWOR there are N(N−1)…(N−n+1) ordered sequences, or C(N,n) unordered subsets when order is ignored.
A sample may be treated as an ordered sequence of draws or as an unordered set. State which interpretation is being used before counting probabilities.

ask.q: Can the ordered sequence 2,2,5 occur under SRSWOR?
ask.nudge: No. A unit cannot be selected twice without replacement.

scenes.title: Why both sample means are unbiased

blocks.body: An estimator is unbiased when its expectation over repeated samples equals the fixed population parameter. We check E(ȳ)=Ȳ.
Each draw Y_j is uniform over the N population values, so E(Y_j)=Ȳ. Therefore E(ȳ)=E[(Y₁+…+Y_n)/n]=Ȳ.
Every population unit has inclusion probability n/N. The sample mean is (1/n)Σ I_i y_i. Hence E(ȳ)=(1/n)Σ(n/N)y_i=Ȳ.

blocks.h: The same conclusion for a proportion
blocks.body: For a characteristic coded 1 if present and 0 otherwise, the sample proportion is a sample mean of zero-one values. It is unbiased under both SRSWR and SRSWOR.

ask.q: Does sampling without replacement make the sample mean biased?
ask.nudge: No. Its expectation still equals the population mean.

scenario.teaser: A small population with different values
scenario.title: Unbiasedness does not depend on replacement
body: Consider a fixed population with values 2, 4 and 6. The population mean is Ȳ=(2+4+6)/3=4. The aim is to estimate this same fixed mean under two different sampling rules.
Under SRSWR, each draw has expected value 4 because every population unit is equally likely on every draw. The draws may repeat, but averaging them still gives expectation 4.
Under SRSWOR, each unit has inclusion probability n/N. The expected sample total is therefore nȲ, and dividing by n gives E(ȳ)=Ȳ. The sample mean is unbiased under this design too.
Thus replacement status does not decide unbiasedness in this example. It changes the joint behaviour of the observations and therefore the variance of the sample mean.
scenario.q: What changes between the designs if both sample means are unbiased?
scenario.answer: Their variances differ because replacement changes dependence between draws.

scenes.title: Variance and the finite-population correction
scenes.objective: Derive and compare the variance formulas.

blocks.body: Let σ²_N=(1/N)Σ(y_i−Ȳ)². Let S²=(1/(N−1))Σ(y_i−Ȳ)². Thus S²=Nσ²_N/(N−1). Always identify which convention is used.
The draws are independent, each with variance σ²_N. Therefore V(ȳ_WR)=σ²_N/n.
The draws are dependent because a selected unit is not returned. The sample mean variance is V(ȳ_WOR)=(1−n/N)S²/n.
The factor (N−n)/(N−1) is at most 1 for 1≤n<N. It equals 1 when n=1 and is strictly below 1 when n>1. At n=N, the census variance is zero.

For SRSWOR, E(p)=P and Var(p)=[(N−n)/(N−1)]·P(1−P)/n. Since p(1−p)=p−p², E[p(1−p)]=E(p)−E(p²)=P−{Var(p)+P²}=P(1−P)−Var(p). Substituting the variance gives E[p(1−p)]=[N(n−1)/(n(N−1))]P(1−P). Therefore, for n>1, an unbiased estimator of P(1−P) is [n(N−1)/(N(n−1))]p(1−p). The finite-population correction here is essential; p(1−p) by itself is biased downward for this target.

blocks.h: Using one known population unit to estimate the total
blocks.body: Suppose y₁ is known exactly. Draw an SRSWOR sample of size n from the remaining N−1 units, with sample mean ȳ₀. Then t₂=y₁+(N−1)ȳ₀ is unbiased for the population total: the known unit is added exactly, and the sample mean estimates the mean of the remaining units. Compare it with t₁=N ȳ from an ordinary SRSWOR sample of size n from all N units. The known-unit construction reduces the variance; under the finite-population variance convention used in the question, Var(t₁)=N²σ²(N−n)/[n(N−1)] and Var(t₂)≤Var(t₁). The sample frame and the finite-population correction must both use N−1 for the second design.

ask.q: Why is the SRSWOR variance smaller for 0<n<N?
ask.nudge: Its variance is the SRSWR variance multiplied by a factor less than one.

flow.title: Compare the sampling designs
flow.alt: Identify replacement status, establish the sample space, select the matching expectation and variance formula, and compare precision.
flow.note: The replacement rule determines whether draws are independent and which variance formula applies.

scenes.title: Worked example: a population of five
scenes.objective: Calculate both variances for a proportion.
scenes.problem: A population has N=5 households. Two households have the characteristic of interest, so P=2/5. Draw n=2 observations. Compare the variance of the sample proportion under SRSWR and SRSWOR.

steps.say: Write the population proportion and its complement.
steps.why: The indicator is one for two households and zero for the other three.

steps.say: Under SRSWR, draws are independent Bernoulli(P).
steps.why: The variance of the average of n independent Bernoulli observations is P(1−P)/n.

steps.say: Apply the finite-population correction for SRSWOR.
steps.why: Without replacement, the sample proportion has the smaller variance.
The SRSWOR variance is lower by the factor 3/4. Both estimators remain unbiased for P=0.4.

ask.q: What is the finite-population correction in this example?

scenes.title: Retrieve the core formulas
scenes.intro: Try each prompt before revealing the answer.

items.q: Can a unit repeat in SRSWR?
items.a: Yes. Each selected unit is returned before the next draw.

items.q: Can a unit repeat in SRSWOR?
items.a: No. Selected units are not returned.

items.claim: The sample mean is unbiased under both SRSWR and SRSWOR.
items.why: Both designs give every draw or selected unit the correct population-average expectation.
Each unit is returned, so the next draw uses the same population composition.
The available population changes after each selection; draws are dependent.

items.claim: SRSWOR always gives a biased sample proportion.
items.why: The sample proportion is unbiased under both designs.

items.claim: For 0<n<N, the SRSWOR variance is lower for the sample mean.
items.why: The finite-population correction is below one.

items.claim: If n=N under SRSWOR, the variance is zero.
items.why: A census observes every population unit.

scenes.title: Transfer: compare two designs
scenes.objective: Apply the FPC to a new sample size.
scenes.problem: A finite population has N=20 units and population variance σ²_N=25. A sample of n=5 is selected. Find the variance of the sample mean under SRSWR and SRSWOR.
hints: For SRSWR, divide σ²_N by n.
For SRSWOR, multiply the SRSWR variance by (N−n)/(N−1).
Calculate the two values and compare.
scenes.check: The without-replacement variance is smaller because 15/19 is less than one.

solution.why: The draws are independent and the population variance is 25.
The correction compares the two sampling designs.

solution.say: Multiply to obtain the without-replacement variance.
solution.why: The result is below five, as expected.

scenes.title: Transfer: a sample proportion
scenes.objective: Apply the two variance formulas to a binary characteristic.
scenes.problem: A population contains N=8 households, of which 3 have a specified characteristic. A sample of n=2 is drawn. Calculate the variance of the sample proportion under SRSWR and SRSWOR.
hints: Set P=3/8 and calculate P(1−P)/n for SRSWR.
For SRSWOR, multiply that result by (N−n)/(N−1).
Keep the exact fractions until the final comparison.
scenes.check: The SRSWOR variance is smaller because the finite-population correction is 6/7.

solution.why: Each draw is an independent zero-one observation with success probability 3/8.
There are fewer remaining units after each draw without replacement.

solution.say: Multiply to obtain the without-replacement variance.
solution.why: The correction is below one, so this variance is smaller than 15/128.

ask.q: What remains unchanged when moving from SRSWR to SRSWOR?
ask.nudge: The sample proportion remains unbiased for the population proportion.

scenes.title: SRSWR and SRSWOR checklist
body: SRSWR returns each selected unit before the next draw. Repeats are possible and draws are independent.
SRSWOR keeps selected units out. Repeats are impossible and draws are dependent.
The sample mean and sample proportion are unbiased under both designs.
For 1≤n<N, the FPC is at most one; it equals one at n=1 and is below one when n>1. A census (n=N) has zero sampling variance under SRSWOR.

ask.q: What are the two formulas you should write before comparing precision?
ask.nudge: Write the SRSWR variance and the SRSWOR variance with its finite-population correction.

scenes.title: Mastery check
scenes.objective: Demonstrate independent command of SRSWR and SRSWOR.

sheet: SRSWR: return each unit; repeats possible; independent draws.
SRSWOR: do not return; no repeats; dependent draws.
FPC is at most one for 1≤n<N; it equals one at n=1 and is zero at a census.
For a zero-one variable, the sample mean is the sample proportion.
SRSWR permits repeated units; SRSWOR does not.
tricks: Identify replacement status before choosing a formula.
Use the variance convention shown in the question.
For a sample proportion, treat each observation as a zero-one variable.
Check n=1: the two designs have the same variance because the FPC equals one.
shortcuts: Both designs are unbiased; variance is the distinguishing property.
For SRSWOR, multiply the matching SRSWR variance by the FPC.
For a proportion, replace the population variance by P(1−P) with the matching FPC convention.
remember: Unbiased does not mean minimum variance.
Do not mix σ²_N and S² without converting the denominator convention.
The FPC equals one when n=1; it is strictly below one only when n>1.
